candidates.label: Tel Lystra, near Hatunsaray
candidates.support: This mound near Hatunsaray was identified as Lystra following the nineteenth-century discovery of a Latin dedicatory inscription naming the Roman colony of Lystra; ToposText and OpenBible.info's catalog independently place the site at the same coordinates. One Wikidata item (not used as a source here) lists a point about 14 km northeast of this location; that entry appears to be a coordinate error rather than a competing scholarly identification, since no published source we found places Lystra there.

summary.text: Lystra was a Roman colony in Lycaonia where, according to Acts, a crowd first hailed Paul and Barnabas as gods after a healing and then, incited by opponents, stoned Paul. Timothy, Paul's later companion, was from Lystra.

scripture.textWEB: they became aware of it and fled to the cities of Lycaonia, Lystra, Derbe, and the surrounding region.
At Lystra a certain man sat, impotent in his feet, a cripple from his mother’s womb, who never had walked.
When they had preached the Good News to that city and had made many disciples, they returned to Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch,
He came to Derbe and Lystra; and behold, a certain disciple was there, named Timothy, the son of a Jewess who believed, but his father was a Greek.
The brothers who were at Lystra and Iconium gave a good testimony about him.
